drills.q: A colleague says 'the p-value was 0.02, so there's a 98% chance our hypothesis is true.' What's wrong with this statement?
drills.a: A p-value is P(data this extreme or more | H0 true), not P(H0 true | data) or P(H1 true | data). Getting from one to the other requires Bayes' theorem and a prior probability on the hypothesis, which the p-value alone doesn't supply.

drills.q: Define Type I and Type II error in one sentence each.
drills.a: Type I: rejecting a true null hypothesis -- a false positive, controlled by alpha. Type II: failing to reject a false null hypothesis -- a false negative, related to power via power=1-beta.

drills.q: You want to compare mean response time across 4 different server configurations. Which test do you run first, and what does a significant result tell you?
drills.a: One-way ANOVA. A significant result tells you at least one configuration's mean differs from at least one other -- it does not tell you which pair(s) differ. Follow with a post-hoc test (Tukey's HSD) to find which configurations differ.

drills.q: Your experiment report tests 20 different metrics and 2 come back significant at raw p<0.05, uncorrected. How suspicious should you be, numerically?
drills.a: Very. At k=20 independent tests each at alpha=0.05, you'd EXPECT about 20*0.05=1 false positive by chance alone even if every null were true, and the family-wise probability of at least one false positive is 1-0.95^20 ~= 64.2%. Two 'hits' out of 20 uncorrected tests is weak evidence; apply Benjamini-Hochberg or Bonferroni correction before trusting them.

drills.q: An A/B test dashboard shows significance on day 3 of a planned 3-week test, and the team ships immediately. What statistical problem does this illustrate, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Peeking -- checking a running experiment and stopping the moment it looks significant inflates the true Type I error rate far above the nominal alpha, since each check is effectively another implicit test. Fix: commit to a fixed sample size/duration decided by a power analysis beforehand, or use a sequential/always-valid testing method designed to control Type I error under continuous monitoring.

drills.q: An A/B test configured for a 50/50 split shows an actual observed split of 55/45 with a chi-square goodness-of-fit p<0.01. What do you do with the experiment's headline result?
drills.a: Treat the experiment as invalidated, not just flag it as a footnote. This is sample ratio mismatch -- it signals a broken randomization/logging/bot-filtering pipeline, and whatever caused the skewed ratio may also have skewed group composition, confounding the treatment effect estimate regardless of what its own p-value shows.

drills.q: Aggregate A/B results show variant B converting worse than A overall, but B wins within every individual traffic segment (mobile, desktop, new users, returning users). Diagnose and explain the likely cause.
drills.a: Simpson's paradox. The aggregate comparison is confounded by unequal segment allocation between arms -- e.g. treatment happened to receive a disproportionate share of a lower-converting segment -- even though each within-segment comparison is clean. Check segment balance between control and treatment before trusting the aggregate number; report segment-level breakdowns as standard practice.

drills.q: You expect a true effect size of Cohen's d=0.1 (very small) but only collected n=200 per group for your test, which came back non-significant. What should you conclude?
drills.a: Little to nothing about whether the effect exists -- detecting d=0.1 at standard alpha=0.05/power=0.80 requires roughly 1,570 per group, so a sample of 200 is drastically underpowered. 'Not significant' here means 'insufficient data to detect it,' not 'no effect' -- report power alongside the null result rather than treating it as evidence of absence.

drills.q: Design the statistical plan for a checkout-flow A/B test expecting a ~1% relative conversion lift, given the team has a history of peeking and post-hoc metric shopping.
drills.a: Pre-register one primary metric and compute required sample size via power analysis using the expected small effect size and historical variance (likely a large sample given how small the effect is). Use a sequential/always-valid testing framework so the team can monitor without inflating Type I error from peeking. Run an automatic SRM check before surfacing any result. Restrict secondary metrics to a pre-declared list with Benjamini-Hochberg correction; treat anything else discovered post-hoc as a new hypothesis for a follow-up experiment. Report segment-level breakdowns to catch Simpson's-paradox-style confounding.

drills.q: You run a chi-square test of independence on a 2x5 contingency table and several expected cell counts are below 5. What's the problem and the fix?
drills.a: Chi-square's p-value relies on a large-sample approximation to the chi-square distribution that becomes unreliable with sparse tables -- a common rule of thumb requires expected count >= 5 in at least 80% of cells. Use Fisher's exact test instead, which computes exact probabilities without relying on that asymptotic approximation.
